header:
Date: 2028-07-19
Time: 09:00 PT
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Jamie Park (Rivermark Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Rivermark Platform Eng), Olivia Reed (Rivermark Security)
Recording: Yes (auto)
Notes: Weekly POC check-in focused on latency tuning (TTFT, streaming, sequence length, kernel choices).
summary: Quick sync to review last week's benchmark changes, discuss streaming vs non-streaming TTFT tradeoffs, and agree next steps: kernel sweep, collect real sequence distribution, and provide security docs. Some audio glitches and a couple of mis-transcribed technical terms (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as 'KV case').
topics: 1) Results from last run: TTFT improvements with streaming and small batch warmup. 2) Kernel choice impact on 4k vs 8k sequences. 3) Sequence length distribution mismatch between test harness and production. 4) Security and network questions for private deployment. 5) Next steps and owners.
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're gonna kick off the weekly rivermark poc sync. Diego's gonna run us through the numbers first, then we can dig into kernel sweeps and sequence length stuff.
[00:10] Jamie Park: Thanks Ava, yep we got Samir and Olivia on. Good to see you all.
[00:22] Diego Morales: Alright I shared the updated benchmark sheet in the chat it's the one with the streaming TTFT column and the new 8k run. Quick tl;dr: streaming reduced TTFT by about 30-35% for the 2k median seqs, for 8k it was smaller but still positive.
[00:35] Samir Patel: Can you remind me which model variant you used for the 8k? Was that the quantized-ggml path or the optimized kernel path?
[00:42] Diego Morales: Yeah so the 8k runs we did last night were on the cuda-optimized kernel set with int8 quantization profile A there was also a fallback run on the nv-compat kernels. The int8 path saved about 22% on token compute but introduced some variance in long-tail latencies.
[00:58] Jamie Park: Right, I noticed the tail latency spikes on some of the 8k tests in the sheet, looked like 99th went up?
[01:05] Diego Morales: Exactly, the 95th is fine but the 99th jumps when the KV cache fills and we hit a kernel that doesn't vectorize well for long sequences that's the kernel choice issue.
[01:18] Olivia Reed: Quick sec from security side we need confirmation that nothing from the payload is logged in plain text, and also can you attach the network diagram? We have to show this to compliance.
[01:27] Ava Chen: Absolutely Olivia, I'll send SOC2 report and the network diagram after the call. It's on our secure docs portal, link incoming.
[01:33] Olivia Reed: Great, thanks.
[01:36] Diego Morales: Back to latency we also ran a small warmup/batch trick: for streaming TTFT we pre-warm the KV cache by sending a ~128 token prefix at low priority, that reduced first-token latency for the next request in the same connection by 15-20%. Not a full fix but helps if you have session affinity.
[01:55] Jamie Park: Hmm that could work for our chat flows, but for stateless webhooks we don't have affinity. Our distribution actually has a big spike at ~300 tokens and a smaller long tail up to 6k. The test harness we're using is mostly 1k-2k which is why your numbers looked better.
[02:12] Diego Morales: Ok that's important can you send the real distribution? We can re-run target runs to match production percentiles.
[02:19] Jamie Park: Yep will do, I'll drop CSV.
[02:25] Samir Patel: Also curious about batching policies if we let Redwood runtime do continuous batching is there a way to cap waiting time so TTFT doesn't become unacceptable?
[02:34] Diego Morales: Yes, we have latency SLO knobs maximum batch delay and priority lanes. For Rivermark we've suggested a 8ms max batch delay for p99 target of 250ms, but that depends on seq length mix. The sheet includes simulated numbers for 4ms/8ms/16ms delays.
[02:50] Jamie Park: What's the effect on cost? If we lower delay we lose batching efficiency right?
[02:56] Diego Morales: Correct, lower delay reduces batching which increases per-token cost. In our simulated runs, moving 8ms -> 4ms increases per-token compute cost by ~12% at current throughput. We'll put exact figures in the updated sheet.
[03:08] Olivia Reed: From a compliance angle, for Dedicated or Private we need to know KMS integration options do you support customer-managed keys?
[03:16] Ava Chen: Yes we support KMS/HSM for Private deployments and dedicated can be configured with customer KMS for encryption at rest. I'll add the integration doc to the link.
[03:24] Jamie Park: Nice. On kernel sweeps Diego, what kernels did you try for 4k vs 8k?
[03:30] Diego Morales: We tried cuda_fused_attention, nv_compat, and our new asm-optimized kernel set (alpha). For 4k, cuda_fused gave best median and tail. For 8k, asm-optimized delivered lower median but had some pathological sequences where nv_compat actually beat it on p99 due to memory-paging differences.
[03:50] Samir Patel: Pathological sequences meaning specific prompt shapes?
[03:54] Diego Morales: Yeah when prompts have lots of separators and repeated tokens the attention patterns change and some kernels don't vectorize well, causing per-step kernel launch overhead to dominate. Also the KV cache becomes larger, evictions may trigger copies.
[04:08] Jamie Park: That's concerning. Can we instrument to see which prompt shapes trigger the p99?
[04:13] Diego Morales: Yep we can do an eval that tags sequences by length and by token-repeat features; we already saw a set of 120 prompts with repeated invoice templates that correlate strongly with spikes. I'll attach that list.
[04:24] Ava Chen: Side note we've seen customers improve TTFT for web UIs by using streaming and early partial renders, so even if p99 is high, perceived latency can be much better. Diego, do we have any demo notes showing streaming partial output for Rivermark's demo flow?
[04:38] Diego Morales: I built a quick demo with partial tokens flushed every 64 tokens; showed a ~200ms earlier visible output for users on median cases. For long tails, streaming helps because the user sees something earlier, but function-calls or structured output needs whole completion so less benefit.
[04:55] Jamie Park: For our use case most are free-text suggestions (we can show partial), but we also have a small portion that needs full, atomic responses for compliance. So hybrid approach maybe.
[05:05] Olivia Reed: For those atomic responses, we need an audit trail of the final response, retention guidelines how long do you keep logs?
[05:12] Ava Chen: Default retention in hosted is 30 days for non-enterprise, but for Dedicated/Private you control retention and we can disable logs. I'll include this in the SOC2/network packet.
[05:22] Samir Patel: Back on kernel sweeps what's the process for us to trigger a dedicated sweep on our pilot cluster? We want to run with our exact docker image and real traffic replay.
[05:31] Diego Morales: We can do an on-prem style sweep in our staging cluster if you provide the replay logs or a SAM pack; otherwise we can give you a runner to run in your env. For privacy you might prefer running it in your VPC in that case we provide a benchmark harness and the kernel binaries.
[05:45] Jamie Park: We'll likely run it in our VPC. Samir will coordinate.
[05:50] Samir Patel: Yup I can set that up, will need the runner docs and the expected resource profile.
[05:54] Ava Chen: I'll attach the runner docs and resource CPU/GPU profiles.
[05:58] Diego Morales: One more note: sequence length padding matters if your real sequences are 300 tokens but the harness pads to 2k, latency is artificially high. We saw that earlier with your tests.
[06:09] Jamie Park: Yeah that was my bad, we were using a canned dataset. We'll send the real distribution tonight.
[06:14] Diego Morales: Great. Regarding TTFT calculation are you measuring from HTTP request start or from websocket open? There's discrepancy.
[06:20] Jamie Park: We're using standard REST call times in the harness.
[06:24] Diego Morales: Ok in our streaming tests TTFT is measured from websocket/frame to first token, so numbers differ. We'll convert metrics so apples-to-apples.
[06:33] Olivia Reed: Also if we go Private, what's the upgrade path? Are kernels signed? We need chain-of-trust for compliance.
[06:39] Ava Chen: Yes, for Private deployments we sign our artifacts and provide an SBOM and signing keys info. I'll include artifact signing and SBOM in the pack.
[06:48] Jamie Park: Any blockers on the perf side before we go to next stage?
[06:51] Diego Morales: Main blockers: we need your real sequence distribution, a list of the top ~200 prompt shapes, and permission to run kernel sweeps in your VPC or give us a replay. Then we can finalize recommendations on kernel choices and batching.
[07:04] Samir Patel: Ok we'll aim to get those by Friday.
[07:08] Ava Chen: Recap then: Diego will run kernel sweep and share latency/cost table; Jamie to send distribution and prompts; Ava to send SOC2, network diagram, runner docs and benchmark sheet update. Schedule on-site perf review propose next Tuesday at 10am PT.
[07:23] Jamie Park: Works for me.
[07:25] Olivia Reed: Works for me.
[07:26] Diego Morales: Quick technical aside for long-tail mitigation we can enable adaptive kernel switching in the runtime so it can fallback to nv_compat when asm-optimized shows tail spikes. It's a config flag in the runtime, we can try it on staging.
[07:40] Jamie Park: That sounds promising. Please include config example.
[07:44] Diego Morales: Will do.
[07:47] Ava Chen: Anything else?
[07:49] Jamie Park: Nothing here. Thanks everyone.
[07:52] Ava Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up via email with the docs and the updated sheet.
[07:57] Samir Patel: Thanks all.
[08:00] End of recording.

Notes: Transcript contains some transcription errors: 'KV case' instead of 'KV cache', occasional speaker mislabels, and missing punctuation. The timing markers are approximate and inserted every 10-90s to reflect meeting cadence.
